item.title: Hermes Birkin bags built their reputation on rarity, but shifting resale demand is changing the conversation
item.description: The Hermes Birkin bag is losing some of its scarcity-driven appeal as second-hand supply grows and resale prices fall from pandemic-era highs. The shift is putting pressure on a luxury business model built around exclusivity, demand and high resale premiums.
item.dc:creator: Trisha Bhattacharya
item.content:encoded: For years, owning a Hermes Birkin bag was about more than carrying an expensive handbag. Its limited availability made it a status symbol, while the prospect of selling it at a substantial profit turned it into an alternative investment for some buyers. That equation, however, is beginning to change. How the Birkin's resale market is changing London-based reseller Cai Baochun, who began selling Birkins online and through social media in 2020, has stopped stockpiling the bags as second-hand prices weaken. “I don’t want to lose money,” he told Reuters.According to Reuters, the resale value of unworn Birkins has fallen by more than $6,000 from its 2022 peak, reflecting a market where increasing availability is putting pressure on the premium buyers once paid to secure the coveted handbags. The change is particularly visible in the Birkin 25, one of the brand's sought-after models. Its unworn black version now sells for around £24,000 on the resale market, according to luxury reseller Antoinette Hunter, founder of Lilac Blue.That is approximately £4,000 below its 2022 price. Cai puts his asking price for the bag at around £20,000, while the same model retails for £9,390 in Britain, Reuters reported.Why scarcity mattered to HermesThe Birkin, named after the late British-French actor Jane Birkin, has long been central to Hermès' luxury positioning. Access to the bag has often been linked to a customer's wider spending at the brand, including purchases of scarves, clothing and shoes.Six resellers told Reuters that this practice remains common, although arrangements vary by region and store.Two resellers estimated that customers might spend between $10,000 and $20,000 on other Hermès products before being offered a Birkin or a Kelly, another sought-after handbag. The company says crafting a Birkin takes 15 hours, but it does not disclose production numbers or its selling policies. Hermes declined to comment to Reuters.For years, the arrangement benefited both the fashion house and the resale market. Customers had an incentive to spend more, while resellers could command substantial premiums from buyers unwilling or unable to obtain a bag directly.Sarah Davis, founder of California-based Fashionphile, described the arrangement as a “win-win”. The company said its Birkin listings have increased 32-fold over 15 years, illustrating how much larger the resale market has become.More bags, weaker premiumsThe expansion of online resale platforms such as Vestiaire Collective and The RealReal has made it easier to buy and sell pre-owned luxury goods. Hermès has also gradually increased production, opening an average of one workshop a year.Together, these developments have made Birkins easier to find on the secondary market. Of nine resellers interviewed by Reuters across the United States, Europe and Asia, six reported falling resale prices over the past year, while five said demand had softened.Brokerage Bernstein said Birkin 25 resale prices averaged around 1.7 times retail in the third quarter, down from 2.6 times at their 2022 peak. UBS analysts, meanwhile, estimated that listings for Birkin and Kelly bags worldwide were six to seven times higher than before the pandemic. The shift matters because Hermès' leather goods division accounts for 44% of group revenue. Its shares had also lost nearly 40% of their market value in 2026, Reuters reported, as investors assessed slower growth and questions about the durability of its scarcity-led strategy. Is the Birkin losing its appeal? Not entirely. Hunter added that demand for the most exclusive Hermes bags remains strong, even as reselling them becomes less profitable. She did however warn that falling resale prices alongside rising retail prices could eventually make buying directly from the brand less attractive. “If Hermes continues to raise the prices, and the prices on the resale market continue to drop, that margin gets squeezed, and perhaps it will become less appealing,” she said. Hermes chief executive Axel Dumas has previously pointed to the limits of expanding production, citing the availability of highly trained artisans and quality leather. Some resellers also report firmer prices for certain bags, suggesting the market is not moving uniformly. The Birkin remains a recognised luxury symbol. However, the question is whether, despite shifts in resale and supply demand, the iconic Birkin can maintain its aura.

item.title: Brazil polls: President Lula da Silva gets 1st smartphone at 80, but can he catch up with Brazil’s digital generation?
item.description: Brazilian President Lula da Silva has got his first smartphone at 80 as he steps up social media campaigning ahead of the presidential runoff. With digital-savvy rivals gaining ground, can the veteran leader connect with Brazil’s younger voters?
item.dc:creator: Bhanu Pratap
item.content:encoded: Just days before his 81st birthday, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva got a new smartphone — reportedly his first ever — as he steps up efforts to connect with voters through social media ahead of a closely watched presidential runoff.“I’m becoming the king of selfies, a real internet user,” Lula told supporters at a recent rally in Brasília, signalling a shift in how the veteran left-wing leader is approaching political campaigning.As Reuters reported, Lula’s smartphone debut comes at a time when social media platforms such as TikTok, Instagram and WhatsApp are increasingly shaping Brazil’s political landscape.The ability to build a large online following and convert digital influence into votes has become a powerful electoral asset, particularly for younger candidates.For Lula, who has spent decades building his political identity through trade unions, grassroots mobilisation and mass rallies, adapting to this new environment could prove crucial as he seeks an unprecedented fourth presidential term.Brazil’s political battle moves onlineThe growing influence of digital campaigning was evident in congressional elections held alongside the first round of this month’s presidential vote. Several younger candidates with strong social media followings performed exceptionally well, according to the report. Lula’s opponent in the runoff is right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.At 45, Flávio has been reaching voters through his own YouTube channel and has emerged as a formidable challenger after topping the first-round vote, surprising pollsters, Reuters reported. Lula learns the social media gameLula, a former shoeshine boy who went on to become a metalworker, trade union leader, and an internationally recognised left-wing politician, first ran for president in 1989. His political communication has historically relied on personal connections with workers, grassroots organisations and supporters at large public gatherings.Ana Elisa Silva, the 21-year-old law student from Minas Gerais, has joined Lula’s inner circle to help him navigate the social media landscape following his disappointing first-round performance, according to Reuters report.Silva told Reuters that the transition required adjustments for a politician who has openly acknowledged his dislike of mobile phones.“This experience remains important, but it needs to align with changes in how people consume information, especially young people.” The rise of ‘influencer politicians’The growing prominence of politicians who have built their own digital audiences marks a further evolution in electoral campaigning, according to Máximo Zaldívar, regional director for Latin America and the Caribbean at the International Foundation for Electoral Systems.Politicians once approached social media personalities to endorse their campaigns. Increasingly, however, candidates themselves are building audiences and political influence through their online content.“The influencer has their own political capital,” Zaldívar said, referring to the followings accumulated across platforms. “That’s what they bring to the table and no politician can compete with that.”Ferreira exemplifies this trend. A staunch Bolsonaro supporter and the son of an evangelical pastor, he has nearly 25 million Instagram followers — equivalent to more than 10% of Brazil’s population.Conservative lawmaker Julia Zanatta, 41, who has more than one million Instagram followers and won over half a million votes in this month’s election, said success on social media requires consistency and a willingness to communicate without being overly concerned about criticism.“I never thought about whether I’d reach more people or if I’d displease anyone,” she said, as per Reuters.With inputs from Reuters.
